articles.label: Infrastructure
articles.headline: Pensacola's $2.1 Million Sidewalk Gap
articles.dek: The city has identified 47 miles of missing sidewalks in high-traffic areas. Three years and two budget cycles later, fewer than six miles have been funded. Where's the holdup?
brief: Pensacola's 2023 pedestrian safety audit identified 47 miles of missing sidewalks near schools, transit stops and commercial corridors
Only 5.8 miles have received funding through two budget cycles, leaving a $2.1 million gap between identified needs and allocated resources
City officials point to competing infrastructure priorities and federal grant timelines while pedestrian advocates push for dedicated funding streams
articles.body:
The crosswalk at Cervantes Street and N Street dead-ends into a drainage ditch. No sidewalk. No shoulder. Just a four-foot drop into standing water and a worn footpath through the grass where hundreds of pedestrians have improvised their own solution.

This gap appeared on Pensacola's pedestrian infrastructure priority list in October 2023. It remains unfunded.

Three years ago, the city completed its first comprehensive pedestrian safety audit in more than a decade. The 78-page document identified 47 miles of missing sidewalks in what it classified as "high-priority" zones—within a quarter mile of schools, public transit stops, parks and commercial districts. The estimated cost to close those gaps: $3.4 million.

Through fiscal years 2024-25 and 2025-26, the city has funded approximately 5.8 miles of new sidewalk construction. That leaves 41 miles unfunded and a gap of roughly $2.1 million between what the audit recommended and what the budget has delivered.

The Math Doesn't Add Up

Pensacola Public Works Director Michael Sykes acknowledged the shortfall at a June budget workshop but framed it as a prioritization issue rather than a funding failure.

"We're not ignoring the audit," Sykes told council members. "We're working through it systematically. But sidewalks compete with stormwater, with roads, with facilities maintenance. Every dollar we put toward pedestrian infrastructure is a dollar we're not putting somewhere else."

The city's current capital improvement plan allocates $400,000 annually for sidewalk construction and repair. At that rate, closing the 47-mile gap would take roughly eight years—assuming costs don't rise and no new gaps are identified.

They will. The audit noted that Pensacola adds approximately 1.2 miles of new "priority gap" each year through development patterns and population shifts.

Federal Money, Local Delays

Part of the holdup is structural. The city has applied for federal Transportation Alternatives Program funding three times since the audit's release. Two applications were denied. The third, submitted in January 2026, remains under review.

TAP grants require a 20% local match, detailed environmental review and compliance with federal accessibility standards that often exceed what the city would build on its own dime. A sidewalk that costs $72 per linear foot with local funds can run $95 or more under federal requirements.

"You're trading speed for scale," said Rachel Dominguez, transportation policy director for the Florida Bicycle Association. "A city can build a quarter mile of sidewalk in three months with local money. The same project with federal funding takes 18 months to two years. But the federal money lets you do five times as much."

Pensacola has opted for local funding on most completed projects, prioritizing speed over scope. The result: faster construction on smaller segments, but a widening gap between what's been done and what the audit said was needed.

Where the Gaps Are

The audit's priority list isn't evenly distributed across the city. The heaviest concentrations of missing sidewalks fall in three areas: the Brownsville neighborhood north of Cervantes Street, the corridor along Mobile Highway between I-110 and Navy Boulevard, and the streets surrounding Warrington Elementary and Middle schools.

All three areas share demographic patterns. Lower median household incomes than the city average. Higher rates of households without vehicle access. More children walking to school.

Escambia County School District data shows that 340 students at Warrington Elementary are classified as "walkers"—living close enough to school that bus service isn't provided. Many of them navigate streets without continuous sidewalks.

"My son walks on the road," said Tanya Brooks, whose 9-year-old attends Warrington Elementary. "There's no other option. The sidewalk just stops at the corner and doesn't pick up again for two blocks."

Brooks has attended three city council meetings to speak during public comment. The section of F Street she's concerned about appeared on the audit's priority list. It has not been funded.

The Political Calculation

Sidewalk construction lacks the political visibility of other infrastructure projects. Ribbon cuttings for new roads draw cameras. Drainage improvements prevent flooding that makes the news. Sidewalks, by contrast, are what one city planner called "invisible until they're missing."

Pensacola City Council member Teniadé Broughton, whose District 7 includes several of the highest-priority gaps, has pushed for a dedicated sidewalk funding stream separate from the general capital improvement budget. Her proposal—a $600,000 annual set-aside—failed in committee during the FY 2025-26 budget process.

"The will isn't there yet," Broughton said. "Everyone agrees we need sidewalks. No one wants to be the one who cut something else to pay for them."

Mayor D.C. Reeves has expressed support for pedestrian infrastructure improvements in general terms but has not backed any specific funding increase. His proposed FY 2026-27 budget, due to council in September, is expected to maintain sidewalk funding at current levels.

What Other Cities Do

Pensacola is not unique in struggling with sidewalk funding, but peer cities have found workarounds. Tallahassee dedicates a portion of its local-option gas tax to pedestrian and bicycle infrastructure. Mobile requires developers to build sidewalks along their property frontage as a condition of permitting. Jacksonville created a neighborhood improvement district that allows residents to tax themselves for infrastructure upgrades including sidewalks.

Pensacola has implemented none of these mechanisms. The city's development code requires sidewalks in new subdivisions but not for infill development or commercial redevelopment in existing neighborhoods—precisely the areas where the audit found the most gaps.

A code amendment proposed in 2024 would have extended sidewalk requirements to commercial projects exceeding $500,000 in value. The Pensacola Council of Neighborhoods supported it. The Greater Pensacola Chamber opposed it, citing construction costs. The amendment was tabled and has not returned to the agenda.

Measuring Progress

By the city's own metrics, pedestrian infrastructure improvements are working where they've been implemented. The Public Works Department reports that pedestrian-involved crashes within 500 feet of completed sidewalk projects dropped 34% in the two years following construction, compared to the two years prior.

That data point appeared in the city's FY 2025-26 budget presentation. It was used to justify the projects already funded, not to argue for expanding funding to address the remaining gaps.

Sykes, the Public Works director, said his department will complete an updated pedestrian audit in early 2027. It will likely identify additional gaps. Whether the funding to address them will follow remains an open question.

At Cervantes and N Street, the footpath through the grass has been worn down to bare dirt. It floods when it rains. People walk it anyway.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The Quiet Land Rush on Perdido Key
articles.dek: At least four large parcels changed hands in the first half of 2026. County records show the buyers share a Tallahassee-based registered agent. What's coming to the key's last undeveloped stretch?
brief: Four parcels totaling 47 acres on Perdido Key sold between January and May 2026 for a combined $31.2 million
All four buyers are LLCs registered to the same Tallahassee agent, who declined to identify the principals
Escambia County planning staff say no development applications have been filed for the properties
articles.body:
The for-sale sign came down from the lot at 16200 Perdido Key Drive sometime in February. No announcement. No press release. The tangle of sea oats and sand pine that had sat on the market for three years simply wasn't for sale anymore.

The buyer, according to Escambia County property records filed February 12, was an entity called PKD Holdings I LLC. Purchase price: $6.8 million for 11.3 acres of Gulf-front land.

Six weeks later, a second parcel sold. Then a third. Then a fourth.

By the end of May, four separate LLCs had acquired a combined 47 acres along a two-mile stretch of Perdido Key's eastern end—the last significant undeveloped corridor on the barrier island. Total consideration: $31.2 million.

All four LLCs share the same registered agent: Coastal Ventures Administrative Services, operating out of a nondescript office park on Thomasville Road in Tallahassee.

Following the Paper

The pattern emerged in county records last month when a title researcher flagged the transactions for a client interested in nearby property.

"Four separate purchases, four separate LLCs, same agent, same timeframe," said Marcus Webb, a commercial real estate attorney in Pensacola who reviewed the filings at The Flightline's request. "That's not coincidental. That's a land assembly."

Land assemblies—where a single buyer acquires multiple adjacent or nearby parcels through different entities—are common in commercial real estate. The structure can prevent sellers from demanding premium prices once they realize a larger project is underway.

The four Perdido Key parcels are not directly adjacent. They're spaced along Perdido Key Drive between the Perdido Key State Park boundary and the Flora-Bama line. But they share characteristics: all are zoned for high-density residential, all have Gulf frontage, and all had been on the market for extended periods.

The Flightline contacted Coastal Ventures Administrative Services three times over two weeks seeking comment. On the third attempt, a woman who answered the phone identified herself as office manager Diane Keller.

"We provide registered agent services for a number of clients," Keller said. "I'm not authorized to discuss the principals of any entity we represent."

Asked whether the four LLCs share common ownership, Keller said, "I can't help you with that."

What the County Knows

Escambia County planning staff confirmed that no development applications, site plans, or rezoning requests have been filed for any of the four parcels.

"Right now they're just vacant land with new owners," said Jennifer Harmon, the county's development services director. "Until someone submits an application, there's nothing for us to review."

The parcels' existing zoning would allow for significant development. Under Escambia County's land development code, high-density residential permits up to 20 units per acre in some configurations. The 47 acres could theoretically support several hundred condominium units, though actual density would depend on setbacks, parking requirements, environmental constraints, and other factors.

Harmon noted that any Gulf-front development would require permits from the Florida Department of Environmental Protection and potentially the Army Corps of Engineers, depending on the scope.

"Barrier island development has gotten more complicated, not less," Harmon said. "Anyone planning something significant out there has a long road ahead."

The Last Stretch

Perdido Key's eastern end has resisted the condo towers that transformed the island's western reaches in the 1980s and 1990s. A combination of factors—state park land, smaller parcel sizes, and the 2008 financial crisis—left this stretch largely undeveloped while projects like Perdido Towers and Beach Colony rose to the west.

Longtime residents describe the area as the key's last holdout.

"When I bought here in 2002, you could stand on the deck and not see another building," said Tom Fitzgerald, who owns a single-family home on Perdido Key Drive about a half-mile from one of the sold parcels. "That's what we came for. That's what we're going to lose."

Fitzgerald said he learned about the sales from a neighbor who'd been tracking property records. No one from any of the purchasing LLCs has contacted nearby property owners, he said.

"We don't know if it's condos, a resort, single-family—nothing," Fitzgerald said. "And apparently nobody has to tell us until they're ready to start building."

Tallahassee Connections

Coastal Ventures Administrative Services, the registered agent for all four LLCs, was incorporated in 2019. Florida Division of Corporations records list a single officer: Bradley Simmons of Tallahassee.

Simmons is a partner at Grayson Simmons Capital, a real estate investment firm that has financed hotel and condominium projects across North Florida. The firm's website lists developments in Jacksonville, St. Augustine, and Panama City Beach.

Reached by phone, Simmons declined to confirm or deny any connection to the Perdido Key purchases.

"Coastal Ventures is a separate administrative services company," Simmons said. "I'm not going to discuss client matters."

Asked whether Grayson Simmons Capital has any interest in Perdido Key development, he said, "We look at opportunities all over the region. I'm not going to get into specifics."

Webb, the real estate attorney, said the structure is deliberately opaque but not unusual.

"You're not going to find a press release," Webb said. "Whoever's behind this wants to control the narrative. They'll announce when they're ready to announce, and not before."

What Happens Next

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes Perdido Key, said he's aware of the transactions but has no information about the buyers' intentions.

"I've heard the speculation," Bergosh said in an interview. "Until there's an application in front of us, it's all speculation."

Bergosh noted that any significant development on the key would face scrutiny from residents and environmental groups that have historically opposed high-density construction on barrier islands.

"There's a process," Bergosh said. "Public hearings, environmental review, traffic studies. Nobody's building a tower out there overnight."

The Perdido Key Association, a property owners group, did not respond to requests for comment.

Meanwhile, the parcels sit empty. The sea oats bend in the Gulf breeze. The sand pines cast their thin shadows.

Whatever is coming to Perdido Key's last quiet stretch, the people who live there will apparently be the last to know.

articles.label: Local News
articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Draws 85,000—and Tests Beach Infrastructure Again
articles.dek: Pensacola Beach reported record Fourth of July crowds for the team's return. Santa Rosa Island Authority staff worked 14-hour shifts. Now comes the debate over who pays for what broke.
brief: An estimated 85,000 visitors flooded Pensacola Beach over the Fourth of July weekend for the Blue Angels' homecoming show, setting a new attendance record.
Santa Rosa Island Authority crews worked 14-hour shifts and burned through six months of maintenance supplies in four days.
SRIA board members are now questioning whether Escambia County should increase its infrastructure contribution for future military aviation events.
articles.body:
The porta-john at the Casino Beach parking lot gave out at 11:47 a.m. Saturday. A line of 30 people had been waiting. The nearest alternative was 400 yards east, past a wall of beach chairs and coolers and sunburned families who had staked their spots before dawn.

By then, the F/A-18 Super Hornets had already made two passes over the crowd. The sound had rattled car windows on Via de Luna. And the Santa Rosa Island Authority maintenance crew was already behind.

"We planned for 70,000," said SRIA Executive Director Paolo Ghio. "We got 85."

The Blue Angels' 2026 homecoming airshow, held over the Fourth of July weekend for the first time since 2019, drew what SRIA officials are calling the largest single-event crowd in Pensacola Beach history. The four-day stretch—Thursday through Sunday—brought an estimated 85,000 visitors to the barrier island, according to traffic counts at the Bob Sikes Bridge toll plaza and beach access parking data.

The show itself ran Friday and Saturday. But the crowds arrived early and stayed late.

The cost of the crush

SRIA staff worked 14-hour shifts Thursday through Sunday. The agency deployed all 23 of its maintenance employees, plus eight contracted laborers. They collected 47 tons of trash—more than double a typical holiday weekend. They replaced 11 damaged trash receptacles, repaired two irrigation line breaks caused by vehicles parking on medians, and responded to four reports of overflowing restroom facilities at public beach access points.

The agency also burned through what Ghio described as roughly six months' worth of routine maintenance supplies in four days: trash bags, cleaning chemicals, replacement parts for restroom fixtures.

"We're not complaining about the turnout," Ghio said. "But the infrastructure took a hit. And that's a cost somebody has to cover."

SRIA operates under Escambia County's authority but manages its own budget through lease revenues, parking fees, and a share of the county's tourist development tax. The agency's current fiscal year budget allocates $1.2 million for maintenance operations. Ghio estimated the homecoming weekend cost the agency between $140,000 and $180,000 in labor, supplies, and equipment wear—figures he said his staff was still finalizing.

Who pays for the show?

The Blue Angels are based at Naval Air Station Pensacola. Their homecoming show is a joint production involving the Navy, Escambia County, Visit Pensacola, and the SRIA. But the cost-sharing arrangement has been a source of friction for years.

Visit Pensacola, the county's tourism marketing arm, promotes the event and coordinates hotel packages. The Navy covers flight operations. Escambia County provides sheriff's deputies for traffic control and some emergency medical services. SRIA handles everything on the sand: trash, restrooms, parking, lifeguards, and the physical condition of the beach itself.

At a June 12 SRIA board meeting, board member Brigette Brooks asked whether the current arrangement was sustainable.

"We love the Blue Angels. Everyone does," Brooks said. "But we're being asked to absorb costs that benefit the whole county, and our budget isn't sized for that."

Escambia County Administrator Wes Moreno did not respond to a request for comment Friday. A spokesperson for Visit Pensacola said the agency was "grateful to all partners" and would participate in any post-event review.

The bridge question

Traffic at the Bob Sikes Bridge toll plaza backed up to Gulf Breeze proper by 8:30 a.m. Friday. The Escambia County Sheriff's Office deployed 14 deputies to manage traffic flow on Via de Luna and at major intersections. ECSO spokesperson Amber Southard said there were no major accidents, though deputies responded to seven fender-benders in beach parking areas and issued 43 parking citations.

The bridge itself handled the load. But SRIA board member Thomas Campanella raised a longer-term concern at the June meeting: what happens when the bridge needs major repairs during peak season?

The Bob Sikes Bridge, built in 1960 and renovated in 1985, is rated "functionally obsolete" by the Florida Department of Transportation, a designation that refers to design limitations rather than structural safety. FDOT's most recent inspection, completed in March, rated the bridge's condition as "satisfactory." But Campanella noted that any closure—even partial—during a Blue Angels weekend would be "a logistical catastrophe."

FDOT spokesperson Tanya Branton said the department had no major work scheduled for the bridge in the current five-year plan.

What's next

SRIA staff will present a full after-action report at the board's July 23 meeting. Ghio said he expected the board to discuss whether to request additional funding from Escambia County for future large-scale events, and whether to revise crowd-management protocols.

"We've done this before. We'll do it again," Ghio said. "But we need to be honest about what it costs."

The Blue Angels' next Pensacola Beach homecoming is tentatively scheduled for July 2027. The Navy has not yet confirmed the date.
